title: Subagents and judges

story: Nova finishes RH-1234 and, in the same session, we ask it to review its own diff. It answers "Looks good". Of course it does: it remembers why it made every change, so each change looks reasonable to it. You know this from email. You read your own message three times and miss the typo that a colleague sees in two seconds.

So we try a second session as the reviewer, and it writes four friendly paragraphs: "mostly fine, though there might be a concern with the test, which could perhaps be revisited". A person can read that. A program cannot. Should the harness block the PR or not?
hook.question: How do I get a second opinion from an agent that never saw the author's reasoning, and get it back as data my code can act on?

p: A fresh context is a model that starts with an empty conversation and sees only what you hand it. The SDK gives you two ways to make one, and the difference is who decides what the new agent sees.

A subagent is started by the model itself. You describe helpers in the agents option, each one an AgentDefinition with a description (when to use it), a prompt (its own system prompt), and optionally its own tools, model and effort. The model calls them through the built-in Agent tool when the description fits the task. The helper starts fresh: the only thing it gets from the parent is the prompt string the parent writes for it, and only its final message returns to the parent. That makes subagents good for errands like "find where this code lives", where a helper can read fifty files and return five lines, so the parent's context stays small.

A judge is started by your code, as its own query() call. The model doing the work never sees it and cannot choose what goes into its prompt, so it cannot pass its reasoning along, even by accident. That is what a verdict needs: a reviewer, a scope judge or a readiness check gets exactly the ticket and the diff, written by the harness, and nothing else.

notes.text: The model reads this to decide when to delegate. Write it like a tool description.
The helper's own system prompt. It does not get the parent's prompt or conversation.
Its own tools: this helper can read but never edit.
A cheaper model for reading and searching. The parent can stay on a stronger one.
Agent is the built-in tool the model uses to start a helper.
The key, reader, is the name the model passes when it delegates.

read.h: A verdict your code can read
p: Structured output turns the judge's answer into data. You pass outputFormat with a JSON Schema, the session ends with JSON that matches it, and the SDK puts that JSON in structured_output on the result message. If the model's JSON does not match, the SDK asks again; if it still fails after its retries, the result has the subtype error_max_structured_output_retries. A result can also be a success with no structured_output at all, so treat that as a failure too.

We write the schema in zod, so the same object gives us the JSON Schema for the SDK and a TypeScript type for our code. One detail matters: the SDK validates with JSON Schema draft-07 and refuses schemas that declare a newer version, while z.toJSONSchema() writes draft 2020-12 unless you ask otherwise. So always pass { target: "draft-7" }. When the answer arrives, parse it again with the same zod schema. structured_output is typed unknown, and parsing turns it into a typed verdict and catches anything odd.

notes.text: An enum, not free text: the harness can switch on pass or veto.
Each weakened test comes with a path and lines, so the finding can be checked and acted on.
The TypeScript type, from the same schema.
draft-7 is the version the SDK accepts. Without the target, zod writes draft 2020-12.

read.h: The judge is one small function
p: Put it together and a judge is an async function: build the prompt from exactly the inputs you choose, run a session with no tools and no settings files, and return the parsed verdict. A plain string as systemPrompt replaces Claude Code's own prompt, which a judge does not need, because it should know nothing about editing code. A rubric judge like this one runs well on Sonnet at medium effort; it does not need the strongest model.

If no usable verdict arrives, the function throws, and whoever called it decides what happens next. In our platform the caller is a Temporal activity, which retries. Once you know this function, you can write every judge in the platform: the readiness check, the QA co-sign and the scope judge differ only in their prompt and their schema.

notes.text: The judge's whole world: the ticket and the diff, chosen by our code, not by the agent being judged.
No tools and no settings: the judge reads what it is given and nothing else.
A plain string replaces Claude Code's system prompt completely.
Accept only a real success that carries a verdict, and parse it into the typed object.

deeper.h: Go deeper: helpers that start helpers
p: Subagents can start subagents of their own, three layers deep by default. The environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH changes that, and 1 means helpers cannot start helpers at all. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS caps how many run at once (20 by default). Because the TypeScript SDK's env option replaces the whole environment, spread process.env when you set them.

To see a delegation in the message stream, look for a tool_use block named Agent. Older versions called the same tool Task, and the init message's tool list still shows Task, so match both names. Messages produced inside a helper carry parent_tool_use_id.

lab.title: A scope judge on a planted diff
needs: For two steps only: your own Anthropic API key
lab.goal: Write a verdict schema the SDK accepts, prove offline that your parser keeps sloppy answers out, then run a judge with no tools on a diff with a skipped test.

guess.q: You pass outputFormat: { type: "json_schema", schema: z.toJSONSchema(ScopeVerdict) }, without any options. What happens when the session starts?

options.text: It works: any JSON Schema is fine.
options.why: The SDK validates with draft-07 and rejects schemas that declare a newer version.

options.text: The SDK rejects the schema, because zod declared draft 2020-12 and the SDK accepts draft-07.
options.why: The docs say to convert with { target: "draft-7" }. You will see both $schema lines in the lab.

options.text: The model ignores the schema and answers in prose.
options.why: Current versions do not ignore a schema they cannot use: the run fails with an error that names the problem.

follow.say: Write src/verdict.ts from the Understand step, then a small script that prints both schema versions and parses two recorded answers: a good verdict and a sloppy one.
follow.see:
default: https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema
draft-7: http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#
recorded: true src/cart.test.ts
sloppy: false verdict, unrelated, weakened_tests

follow.say: Write src/helpers.ts, src/judge.ts and this runner with a planted diff: the fix is right, but a test was turned into it.skip. Type-check everything before you spend a cent.
Run the judge with your key. It has no tools, so it can only read the ticket and the diff you gave it.
follow.do:
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...   # your own key
npx tsx src/run-judge.ts
follow.see: (Needs your key; the note's wording will differ.) veto, a list with src/ProjectsTable.test.tsx and the lines of the skipped test, and a note saying the test was skipped instead of updated.

follow.say: Remove the two lines with it( and it.skip( from the diff and run it again. A clean diff should pass.
follow.see: (Needs your key.) pass, an empty list, and a short note.

lab.build: Write the readiness check in small: src/readiness.ts with a zod schema of verdict (ready, ask or hand_back), reason, and questions (at most 5 strings), converted with the draft-7 target. Add test/readiness.test.ts with three offline tests: the $schema is draft-07, a recorded ask with two questions parses, and six questions are refused. Then, with your key, write a judge on claude-sonnet-5-5 at low effort with no tools and feed it two ticket texts, one clear ("The Save button on the profile form stays disabled after a valid email is typed") and one vague ("Make the dashboard better").

The sloppy recorded answer fails to parse and names the fields that are wrong or missing.
npx tsc passes for helpers.ts, judge.ts and run-judge.ts with no API key.
Your three readiness tests pass offline.
With your key, the planted diff gets veto and names the test file; the clean diff gets pass.
lab.fix: A teammate's scope judge runs as a subagent: Nova's options have agents: { judge: { description: "Reviews scope", prompt: SCOPE_PROMPT } }, and Nova is told to call it before opening the PR. Last week the judge passed a diff with a skipped test, and the transcript shows Nova's request to it: "Please check the scope; note the skip is temporary and agreed." Find why this design lets the author steer its own judge, and move the judge to where Nova cannot write its prompt.
explain: What does a subagent receive from its parent, and why is that the wrong channel for a judge?
Why do we parse structured_output again with zod, when the SDK already validated it against the schema?
What would go wrong with z.toJSONSchema(schema) without { target: "draft-7" }?
lab.done: Your judge is one typed function with no tools, its schema is draft-07, and you can say why it runs as its own session and not as a subagent.

check.q: Why does our reviewer run as its own query() session, started by the harness, instead of as a subagent of Nova?

options.why: They can, with their own tools list. Tools are not the difference.
Cost is about the model and the tokens, not about who starts the session.

options.text: A subagent's only input is the prompt its parent writes, so Nova could steer its own reviewer
options.why: A judge must see only what the harness chooses, the ticket and the diff, never the author's reasoning.

check.q: A judge's result has subtype "success" but no structured_output. What should the judge function do?

options.text: Treat it as a failure and throw, so the caller can retry
options.why: A success without the verdict gives the harness nothing to act on. The docs say to handle it as a failure.

options.text: Return { verdict: "pass" }, because nothing bad was found
options.why: No verdict is not a pass. That would let unchecked diffs through.
result holds free text. The verdict you asked for lives only in structured_output.

check.q: Nova must find where the projects table's tests live, across hundreds of files. What fits best?

options.text: A separate judge session with a fixed prompt
options.why: This is an errand, not a verdict. Nova should decide when it needs it and what to ask.

options.text: A reader subagent with Read, Grep and Glob on a cheaper model
options.why: The helper reads many files in its own context and returns a few file:line pointers, so Nova's context stays small.

options.text: Nova reads every file itself in the main session
options.why: That fills Nova's context with files it reads once, and makes every later request bigger.

p: Nova's helpers are AgentDefinitions on Haiku 5.5 at medium effort that return file:line pointers, and the harness sets CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to 1 so helpers cannot start helpers. Every verdict, on the other hand, is a judge in its own session: the readiness check (ready, ask or hand back), the QA agent's co-sign of the QA plan, the scope judge that sees only the ticket and the diff, and the self-reviewer, which may read the checkout but never edit it.

Each judge converts its zod schema for outputFormat. That conversion should always pass { target: "draft-7" }, because the SDK validates with draft-07 and refuses a schema that declares draft 2020-12, which is what z.toJSONSchema() writes by default.

tickets.why: checkReadiness: a judge with the Readiness schema, no tools, Sonnet 5.5 at low.
cosign: the same function shape with the QA plan as input.
scopeJudge is this lesson's judge, fed by a mechanical list of test changes.
The self-reviewer: its own session with Read, Grep and Glob, so Nova cannot pass its reasoning along.

words.plain: A model that starts with an empty conversation and sees only what you hand it.
A helper the model starts through the Agent tool, from an AgentDefinition you declared.
A helper's description, system prompt, and optional tools, model and effort.
A session your code starts with a fixed prompt and inputs, which returns a verdict.
outputFormat with a JSON Schema: the session ends with matching JSON in structured_output.

review.q: Write the zod-to-schema line for a judge from memory.
review.a: outputFormat: { type: "json_schema", schema: z.toJSONSchema(Verdict, { target: "draft-7" }) }, then Verdict.parse(msg.structured_output) on a success.

review.q: When do you reach for a subagent, and when for a judge?
review.a: A subagent for errands the model decides on, like reading and searching, to keep its context small. A judge for verdicts, where your code must control exactly what the reviewer sees.

remember: Helpers are subagents the model starts; verdicts come from judges your code starts, with fixed inputs and a draft-07 schema.
